Volume 12 · Chapter 01

Identification, estimands and asymptotic tools

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v02, v03, v04, v05

By the endSeparate what data identify from what an estimator computes and justify limiting arguments.

Volume 12 · Chapter 1

Identification, estimands and asymptotic tools

An automated invoice system flags 60% of invoices as late. A larger database can measure that flag frequency very precisely. It does not, by itself, reveal the fraction actually paid late: the recording rule can make false positive and false negative errors. Econometric reasoning begins by deciding what the target means, which observable law can determine it, and what assumptions connect the two. Only then does a standard error become informative.

Capability. Define an estimand and its identifying assumptions; construct observationally equivalent models; prove consistency using an explicit separation and uniform-convergence argument; manipulate stochastic orders with their quantifiers; and derive regular and nonregular limits with the correct sampling variance. The financial and economic illustrations are original synthetic cases.

Prerequisites. Compactness, derivatives, Taylor remainders and matrix algebra from Volume 2; the integrable weak law, finite-variance scalar central limit theorem and Slutsky argument proved in Volume 3, Chapter 6; estimation and inference from Chapter 7 and Chapter 8; and the provenance, projection and identification distinctions of Volume 4, Chapter 1, Chapter 7 and Chapter 8. Volume 5 supplies the economic interpretation of choices and counterfactuals. No dependent-data or high-dimensional central limit theorem is assumed.

1. The target, the observable law and the estimate

A statistical model is a collection of possible data-generating mechanisms. Write m for a mechanism, Pm for its observable-data law, and θ(m) for the target. The target, or estimand, is a specified population quantity, not the number returned by a computer. An estimator θ̂n=Tn(W₁,…,Wₙ) is a measurable rule applied to a sample. Its realized value is an estimate. The sampling unit, population, measurement date, outcome units and any treatment intervention belong in the target definition.

The target is point identified in the model if Pm=Pm′ implies θ(m)=θ(m′). Equivalently it is a single-valued functional of the observable law within that model. At a particular observable law P, the identified set is Θ(P)={θ(m):Pm=P}. A nonsingleton set describes partial identification. A target may be point identified in a restrictive model and unidentified in a larger model. Identification refers to knowledge of the entire observable law, not to whether a particular finite sample has enough rows for an optimization algorithm.

Why nonidentification blocks universal consistency. Suppose two admissible mechanisms induce the same iid sample law for every n but have targets θ₁≠θ₂. Choose disjoint balls of radius less than ‖θ₁−θ₂‖/2 around the targets. If the same estimator were consistent under both mechanisms, the probability of lying in each ball would tend to one under the same sample distribution. Their probabilities sum to at most one, a contradiction. Additional observations from the unchanged measurement process cannot solve this problem. New identifying information, a smaller justified model, or a set-valued conclusion is necessary.

Worked example 1: a recording error is not sampling noise

Let L be the unobserved indicator of actual late payment and D the recorded flag. Define θ=P(L=1), false positive rate α=P(D=1|L=0), and false negative rate β=P(D=0|L=1). A fresh invoice is an iid draw from this population. The observable success probability is p=P(D=1)=α+(1−α−β)θ. With known α=.1 and β=.2, the denominator d=1−α−β=.7 is nonzero and

θ=(p−α)/(1−α−β). At p=.6, θ=5/7≈.714286.

Now allow the error rates to be unknown. The mechanism (α,β,θ)=(.2,.1,4/7) gives exactly the same Bernoulli(.6) law for D as (.1,.2,5/7). Both define valid joint distributions of (L,D). Even the infinite sequence of iid flags has the same observable law in the two worlds. A claim that the true late share is .6 simply assumes away both error types.

Suppose external validation establishes only α∈[.05,.15] and β∈[.15,.25]. Throughout this rectangle, d>0, the implied θ is admissible, ∂θ/∂α=(p+β−1)/d²<0 and ∂θ/∂β=(p−α)/d²>0 at p=.6. Consequently the sharp identified set is

Θ(P)=[(.6−.15)/(1−.15−.15), (.6−.05)/(1−.05−.25)]
=[9/14,11/14]≈[.642857,.785714].

Both endpoints are attained by permissible recording mechanisms. The continuous image of the connected error-rate rectangle contains every value between them, so these are sharp bounds, not merely outer bounds. This set presumes exact knowledge of p=.6; a finite-sample confidence procedure must also allow uncertainty in p and, if relevant, in the validation bounds. Increasing only the flag sample cannot eliminate the interval's identification width 1/7.

If α+β=1, D has success probability α for every θ: the flag carries no information about actual lateness. If α+β is close to one, inversion amplifies sampling and calibration errors. A negative d can still identify θ when the error rates are known; its sign reverses the relation between flags and true lateness. The examples below use the stated positive d. A conditional mean, projection coefficient or predictive probability can be well defined and identified from observables without identifying a causal intervention. Always state the extra counterfactual restriction before calling a descriptive contrast an effect.

2. Convergence and orders with explicit quantifiers

For a random vector Xₙ and fixed vector x, Xₙ→Px means P(‖Xₙ−x‖>ε)→0 for every ε>0. Any fixed norm in finite dimension is equivalent for this purpose. Convergence in distribution Xₙ⇒X concerns the distributions; it does not assert that Xₙ and X become close on the same realized path. Distributional convergence to a constant does imply convergence in probability to that constant. Almost sure and mean-square convergence are stronger, different statements; neither is implied by probability convergence without additional assumptions.

Let aₙ>0 be deterministic. Write Xₙ=oP(aₙ) if Xₙ/aₙ→P0. Write Xₙ=OP(aₙ) if for every ε>0 there exist finite M and N such that P(‖Xₙ‖>Maₙ)<ε for all n≥N. This is an eventual probability bound, not a deterministic bound for every sample and not a bound on expectations. The norm matters: a one-sided upper bound would incorrectly describe the deterministic sequence −n as bounded.

An iid mean with finite variance satisfies X̄ₙ−μ=OP(n−1/2) by Chebyshev or the CLT. The centering cannot be omitted when μ≠0. A fixed nondegenerate normal variable Z, used for every n, is OP(1) but not oP(1). Conversely, take Xₙ=n with probability 1/n and zero otherwise. Then Xₙ→P0 and is OP(1), but E|Xₙ|=1 and E[Xₙ²]=n. None of these convergence statements licenses convergence of moments.

Order algebra without independence. If Uₙ=OP(1) and Vₙ=oP(1), choose M so P(‖Uₙ‖>M)<ε/2 eventually. For any η>0,

P(‖UₙVₙ‖>η)≤P(‖Uₙ‖>M)+P(‖Vₙ‖>η/M), with limsup at most ε/2.

Here the product is scalar, matrix-vector, or another product with a submultiplicative compatible norm; take M>0. Since ε is arbitrary, UₙVₙ=oP(1). The same union bound shows that a sum of two OP(1) sequences and a product of two OP(1) sequences are OP(1). Rescaling yields OP(aₙ)oP(bₙ)=oP(aₙbₙ). Dependence between the factors is allowed. A denominator needs more: Aₙ→Pa≠0 implies 1/Aₙ→P1/a, with any arbitrary definition on zero-denominator events whose probability tends to zero. Merely Aₙ=OP(1) does not justify inversion.

Continuous transformations at a constant. If Tₙ→Pt and g is continuous at t, choose δ so ‖u−t‖≤δ implies ‖g(u)−g(t)‖≤ε. The probability of the latter error is then bounded by P(‖Tₙ−t‖>δ). This proves the continuous mapping step used for plug-ins. Matrix inversion is continuous near a nonsingular fixed matrix A: the determinant remains nonzero in a sufficiently small neighborhood, and A−1=adj(A)/det(A) has continuous entries there. Thus entrywise consistent fixed-size covariance or Gram estimates can be inverted when their population limit is nonsingular; sample singularities outside the neighborhood become negligible. A growing matrix dimension or an eigenvalue tending to zero requires a different argument.

Mikusheva's limit-theorem notes provide the standard stochastic-order and limiting framework. The definitions and arguments here keep centering, absolute values and exceptional events explicit.

3. Consistency requires a target and control of the whole criterion

An estimator is consistent for θ₀ under P if θ̂ₙ→Pθ₀. This is a statement at a specified data-generating law. It does not show that θ₀ is the policy target of interest. For example, minimizing squared prediction error may consistently estimate a best linear projection even when a structural model is misspecified. The pseudo-true value is the minimizer of the population criterion actually used, rather than a parameter recovered by asserting that the model must be true.

Consider a nonempty compact parameter set Θ⊂ℝk, a continuous deterministic population criterion Q(θ), and a unique minimizer θ₀. Let Qₙ be a random criterion satisfying Δₙ=supθ∈Θ|Qₙ(θ)−Q(θ)|→P0. Assume this supremum and the selected estimator are measurable. The estimator may be an approximate minimizer:

Qₙ(θ̂ₙ)≤infθ∈ΘQₙ(θ)+rₙ, where θ̂ₙ∈Θ and 0≤rₙ=oP(1).

Compact extremum consistency proof. Fix ε>0. The set Θε={θ∈Θ:‖θ−θ₀‖≥ε} is compact. If it is empty the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise continuity gives an attained minimum of Q there. Uniqueness implies the gap ηε=infΘεQ−Q(θ₀)>0. The approximate-minimizer inequality gives

Q(θ̂ₙ)≤Qₙ(θ̂ₙ)+Δₙ≤Qₙ(θ₀)+rₙ+Δₙ≤Q(θ₀)+2Δₙ+rₙ.

Therefore P(‖θ̂ₙ−θ₀‖≥ε)≤P(2Δₙ+rₙ≥ηε)→0. This proves consistency. It uses identification of a unique criterion minimizer, uniform approximation, controlled numerical error, and the parameter-domain conditions separately. It does not say that every criterion minimizer has a causal interpretation. The compact argument and its identification cautions are treated in Chernozhukov's extremum-estimation notes.

If Q(θ)−Q(θ₀)≥c‖θ−θ₀‖² for c>0, the same argument gives ‖θ̂ₙ−θ₀‖≤[(2Δₙ+rₙ)/c]1/2. For Δₙ=OP(n−1/2) and rₙ=OP(n−1), this bound supplies only OP(n−1/4). It does not prove a root-n rate. Sharper local score and curvature arguments often improve the rate, but they must be supplied. A fixed optimization tolerance r>0 leaves a nonvanishing error bound; an optimizer's success message alone does not establish consistency.

Worked example 2: pointwise convergence misses the moving minimum

Let Θ=[0,1], Q(θ)=θ² and, for n≥2, Qₙ(θ)=θ²−2I{1−1/n≤θ≤1−1/(2n)}. For any fixed θ<1, the shrinking dip is eventually to its right; θ=1 is always outside it. Thus Qₙ(θ)→Q(θ) at every fixed θ. The population minimizer is zero.

Inside the dip, θ²−2<0, while outside it θ²≥0. Squaring is increasing on this positive interval, so the unique sample minimizer is θ̂ₙ=1−1/n. It converges to one, the wrong answer. Moreover sup|Qₙ−Q|=2 for every n. Nothing stochastic is needed to demonstrate the failure. Continuity of Qₙ was not a hypothesis of the preceding theorem; its failure here does not explain away the missing uniform convergence. Pointwise checks at any fixed finite list of parameter values eventually miss the dip.

A sufficient uniform law, proved by a finite net. Suppose Wᵢ are iid, Θ is compact, and q(W,θ) is measurable in W and continuous in θ. Let Qₙ(θ)=n−1Σq(Wᵢ,θ), Q(θ)=E[q(W,θ)]. Assume E|q(W,θ*)|<∞ for one θ*∈Θ and a nonnegative integrable random L(W) with |q(W,θ)−q(W,θ′)|≤L(W)‖θ−θ′‖ for all θ,θ′. Compactness gives a finite δ-net θ₁,…,θJ. Every θ is within δ of a net point, so

supΘ|Qₙ−Q|≤maxj≤J|Qₙ(θⱼ)−Q(θⱼ)|+δ[PₙL+EL],
PₙL=n−1ΣL(Wᵢ).

The Lipschitz bound and finite diameter make q(W,θⱼ) integrable. For fixed δ and its finite net, the weak law plus a union bound makes the first term vanish in probability; PₙL→PEL. Given a target tolerance, choose δ small enough that δ(2EL+1) is below half that tolerance, then take n large. This proves uniform convergence. It also gives continuity of Q through |Q(θ)−Q(θ′)|≤EL‖θ−θ′‖. A countable dense subset of compact Θ produces the same supremum for these continuous sample paths, establishing measurability. A measurable approximate minimizer remains an explicit selection assumption unless a particular estimator is constructed. This proof is a sufficient iid finite-dimensional result, not a theorem for every empirical process.

4. From stochastic expansion to a sampling distribution

Let ψ(W) be a fixed k-vector with Eψ=0 and E‖ψ‖²<∞. An asymptotically linear estimator has an expansion

√n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀)=n−1/2Σψ(Wᵢ)+oP(1).

For a fixed row vector a′, the scalar variables a′ψ(Wᵢ) are iid, centered and have variance a′Σa, where Σ=E[ψψ′]. The scalar CLT from Volume 3, followed by Slutsky for the remainder, gives a′√n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀)⇒N(0,a′Σa). If this variance is zero, that projection is zero almost surely before the remainder and its limit is the constant zero. These projection arguments establish every linear contrast. The covariance Σ is positive semidefinite; its square root A from Volume 2 constructs a candidate AZ using independent standard normal coordinates, with covariance AA′=Σ. The finite-dimensional Cramér–Wold characterization then turns the established limits of every linear projection into the joint normal statement N(0,Σ). That general weak-convergence characterization is invoked here, not newly proved; the contrast results used below follow directly from the proved scalar CLT. The fixed-dimensional iid vector CLT is also stated in the cited MIT limit notes. This route does not establish a dependent-data or growing-dimension result.

Even before using the CLT, E‖n−1/2Σψᵢ‖²=trace(Σ) gives OP(1) by Markov's inequality. Thus the expansion implies θ̂ₙ−θ₀=OP(n−1/2) and consistency. The displayed limiting covariance is not automatically the limit of the finite-sample covariance of √n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀): the remainder can be small in probability while having large moments. Moment convergence needs separate control such as appropriate uniform integrability.

Studentization. For a scalar asymptotic variance V>0 and V̂ₙ→PV, Slutsky yields √n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀)/√V̂ₙ⇒N(0,1), defined arbitrarily when V̂ₙ≤0 if such events become negligible. A reported standard error is √(V̂ₙ/n), not √V̂ₙ. To estimate the variance of an iid scalar mean, finite second moments suffice: the integrable weak law applies to X² even if X has no fourth moment. Therefore n−1ΣXᵢ²−X̄ₙ²→PVar(X). Independence between the estimated mean and variance is unnecessary for asymptotic studentization.

An influence-function variance estimator using estimated ψ̂ᵢ needs more than a label. One sufficient route is n−1Σ‖ψ̂ᵢ−ψᵢ‖²=oP(1). Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the average cross products by the square root of this error times the square root of n−1Σ‖ψᵢ‖²=OP(1); the squared-error term also vanishes. Hence n−1Σψ̂ᵢψ̂ᵢ′−n−1Σψᵢψᵢ′=oP(1), entrywise or in a fixed-size matrix norm. The integrable weak law gives the latter average's limit Σ. Verifying the estimated-influence error depends on the estimator; it is not automatic.

5. Delta methods carry the derivative and the covariance

Suppose √n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀)=OP(1) and g:ℝk→ℝr is differentiable at θ₀, with derivative matrix G. Differentiability means g(θ₀+h)−g(θ₀)=Gh+R(h), where ‖R(h)‖/‖h‖→0 as h→0; set that ratio to zero at h=0. Consistency gives this ratio evaluated at θ̂ₙ−θ₀ as oP(1). The order-product proof therefore yields

√n[g(θ̂ₙ)−g(θ₀)]=G√n(θ̂ₙ−θ₀)+oP(1).

This proves the first-order delta expansion. Under the asymptotically linear representation, each scalar contrast has influence equal to the corresponding row of Gψ and variance given by GΣG′. Continuous differentiability on an entire neighborhood is unnecessary for this remainder argument; differentiability at the limiting parameter is enough. A zero derivative can make the root-n limit degenerate, and a zero or nearly zero denominator can invalidate the assumed regular neighborhood. Kempthorne's consistency and delta-method notes discuss these transformations and studentized limits; the applications and calculations here are original.

Worked example 3: corrected prevalence and validation uncertainty

Return to known α=.1, β=.2 and true p=.6. Use θ̂=(D̄−.1)/.7. The iid Bernoulli CLT gives √n(θ̂−5/7)⇒N(0,24/49). Its consistent variance estimate is V̂=D̄(1−D̄)/(.7)². With n=400 and observed D̄=.6,

SE=√6/70≈.034992711.
θ̂±z.975SE≈[.645701262,.782870167], using z.975≈1.959963985.

This is a nominal 95% asymptotic Wald interval under the stated model, not a 95% probability that a fixed θ moves randomly after the data are observed. Before sampling, repeated intervals have coverage tending to .95 at this fixed interior law. The untruncated estimator can fall outside [0,1] in finite samples. Projecting it onto [0,1] is consistent because projection is continuous; at an interior true θ its value agrees with the untruncated estimate with probability tending to one, so the regular limit remains valid.

Now suppose α and β are themselves estimated from two independent validation strata: n truly nonlate invoices for the false positive rate and n truly late invoices for the false negative rate, independent of the main sample. True labels in these strata are known without error by assumption. At the displayed law the gradient of g(p,α,β)=(p−α)/(1−α−β) is (10/7,−20/49,50/49). Independence makes the covariance matrix diagonal with entries .24, .09 and .16 for the three root-n sample proportions. Thus

V=(10/7)²(.24)+(20/49)²(.09)+(50/49)²(.16)=1612/2401,
SE at n=400 ≈ .040969102.

Treating the estimated rates as known would understate uncertainty in this case. If validation sample sizes nα/n→κα>0 and nβ/n→κβ>0, divide their respective variance contributions by κα and κβ. Overlapping samples require covariance terms; unrepresentative validation requires a new identification argument. The three independent samples here can be grouped into iid triples of Bernoulli observations, so the scalar influence CLT applies without an additional sampling theorem.

At the boundary θ₀=0, take α=.1, β=.2 as the stipulated recording kernel, including its hypothetical rule for the absent late class. Then p=.1 and the untruncated corrected estimator has root-n limit Z∼N(0,9/49). The projected estimator instead has limit max(0,Z), with probability mass 1/2 at zero. It is consistent, but ordinary interior normal inference does not describe it. For a proof, note that with probability tending to one the upper bound never binds; the lower-bound map is exactly the positive part, a continuous function. More data do not turn that boundary limit into a centered normal law.

Worked example 4: a ratio whose numerator and denominator are dependent

Let D indicate service use and Y be a cost outcome. The estimand is μ=E[Y|D=1], a descriptive conditional mean. Write A=DY so μ=EA/ED when p=ED>0. The complete law of (A,D) is (0,0) with probability .6, (2,1) with probability .2 and (8,1) with probability .2. Unused-service outcomes are irrelevant to this target; this law supplies no potential-outcome comparison.

Here EA=2, ED=2/5, μ=5, Var(A)=48/5, Cov(A,D)=6/5 and Var(D)=6/25. The ratio estimator is μ̂=Ā/D̄, defined as zero if D̄=0; that event has probability (.6)n and becomes negligible. The gradient of g(a,p)=a/p is (5/2,−25/2). Including both covariance terms gives

V=(5/2)²(48/5)+2(5/2)(−25/2)(6/5)+(−25/2)²(6/25)
=60−75+75/2=45/2.

The same result follows from the influence ψ=(A−μD)/p=D(Y−5)/(.4), which takes values 0, −15/2 and 15/2 with probabilities .6,.2,.2. It is centered and has variance 45/2. The exact algebra μ̂−μ=Pₙ(A−μD)/D̄, followed by D̄→Pp, proves the linearization directly. A plug-in influence variance is Pₙ[(Aᵢ−μ̂Dᵢ)²]/D̄²; finite support, sample-frequency consistency and p>0 establish its consistency here.

For n=500 with counts 300,100,100, μ̂=5 and V̂=45/2. The standard error is √(.045)≈.212132034 and the nominal 95% interval is [4.584228853,5.415771147]. Incorrectly treating Ā and D̄ as independent would use variance 195/2 instead of 45/2. A correctly calculated descriptive interval still does not establish the causal effect of service use.

6. Zero derivatives, weak information and finite coverage

Worked example 5: squared mean profit

Let iid profit observations have mean μ, finite variance σ²>0, and estimator X̄ₙ. The target is τ=μ², not E[X²]. For μ≠0, the delta method gives √n(X̄ₙ²−μ²)⇒N(0,4μ²σ²). At μ=0, the first derivative vanishes and the root-n limit is the constant zero. The exact identity provides the useful next rate:

nX̄ₙ²/σ²=(√nX̄ₙ/σ)²⇒Z², where Z∼N(0,1).

Z² has the chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom. The passage follows by the continuous square map; it does not require normal observations or a fourth moment. It describes distributions, not convergence of the estimator's second moment. If observations are actually N(μ,σ²), the standardized mean is normal exactly. Along local means μₙ=c/√n, nX̄ₙ²/σ² has the exact law (Z+c/σ)², while the centered scaled error n(X̄ₙ²−μₙ²)/σ² has law Z²+2(c/σ)Z. Neither is the regular fixed-nonzero-μ normal approximation uniformly near zero.

Weak identification along a sequence of models. Suppose Yᵢ=λθ+εᵢ, iid εᵢ∼N(0,1), with known λ>0. Every fixed λ identifies θ from EY/λ, and θ̂=Ȳ/λ has variance 1/(nλ²), tending to zero. But along λₙ=n−1/2, θ̂−θ has the exact N(0,1) law for every n. It is not consistent along this sequence. More generally its precision is controlled by nλₙ²: this tends to infinity only when the information grows sufficiently fast. Point identification at every member of a sequence does not supply uniform statistical precision.

This is different from the uniform-in-θ criterion convergence used in the extremum proof. There, the supremum ranges over candidate parameters for one sampling law. A uniform-over-model coverage or consistency claim requires a supremum over possible data-generating laws, possibly including weakly informative ones. A theorem proved at each fixed, well-behaved law does not establish the latter.

Finite coverage can be checked under a fully specified finite model. For Bernoulli data with true p=.6, let K be the success count and use the Wald interval K/n±z.975√[(K/n)(1−K/n)/n]. Its exact coverage under that law is

Σk=0n C(n,k)(.6)k(.4)n−k
×I{|k/n−.6|≤z.975√[(k/n)(1−k/n)/n]}.

Direct enumeration gives approximately .936246277 for n=25, .948117979 for n=100, and .947392305 for n=400. The finite-n coverage need not equal .95 or improve monotonically in n. The same coverage applies to the affine corrected-share interval with fixed known α=.1 and β=.2 because the positive affine transformation preserves the coverage event. These are exact finite-law sums evaluated numerically, not a simulation and not a bound valid for every p. The CLT still establishes pointwise coverage tending to .95 for fixed p∈(0,1). No universal “n exceeds 30” condition follows.

A computational audit should therefore record the target, model, sampling law, exceptional events, approximation and criterion used to judge error. Precision in an estimate of a recorded flag cannot repair a measurement assumption; a robust standard error cannot repair a causal exclusion restriction; and a correct limit theorem cannot turn a selected significant result into a pre-specified test.

Exercises

For each derivation, state the sampling law and the probability claim before calculating. Problems 3–6 require proofs; Problems 10–12 require a critique as well as a numerical or theoretical result. All questions are original.

  1. In the invoice model with observable p=.6, construct the two joint laws corresponding to (α,β,θ)=(.1,.2,5/7) and (.2,.1,4/7). Give all four cell probabilities in each law. Verify the identical observable law and different targets. With α∈[.05,.15], β∈[.15,.25], derive the sharp identified interval and explain why it is not a finite-sample confidence interval.
  2. Let U be uniform on (0,1) and Xₙ=nI{U≤1/n}. Prove probability and almost sure convergence to zero, calculate E|Xₙ| and Var(Xₙ), and decide whether Xₙ=oP(1) and OP(1). Explain why these answers do not justify a variance-convergence claim. Then show that a fixed standard normal Z is OP(1) but not oP(1).
  3. Prove OP(aₙ)OP(bₙ)=OP(aₙbₙ) without independence, and prove that Aₙ→Pa≠0 permits inversion with an arbitrary definition on Aₙ=0. Give a sequence that is OP(1) whose reciprocal is not OP(1). State a corresponding condition for inversion of a fixed-size random matrix.
  4. Suppose Q(θ)−Q(θ₀)≥4‖θ−θ₀‖² and an approximate minimizer has Δₙ≤.002 and rₙ≤.001 on an event Eₙ. Bound its parameter error on Eₙ. If P(Eₙ)≥.97, what finite probability statement follows? For general Δₙ=OP(n−1/2) and rₙ=OP(n−1), derive the rate supplied by this argument and explain why a root-n claim is unsupported.
  5. Prove every assertion in the moving-dip counterexample. A reviewer checks Qₙ at θ=0,.25,.5,.75,1 for increasingly large n and sees convergence. Explain why this is insufficient and identify exactly which extremum-consistency hypothesis fails.
  6. For iid scalar W with EW²<∞ and Θ=[−B,B], B>0, apply the finite-net theorem to q(W,θ)=(W−θ)². Supply an integrable Lipschitz bound, derive Q(θ), identify its unique minimizer even when EW lies outside Θ, and explain why consistency alone does not show that this minimizer is an economically structural parameter.
  7. Recompute the corrected-share standard error at n=400, p̂=.6 with known α=.1,β=.2. Then derive the gradient and the variance when the two independent validation strata each have size n. If instead their sample-size ratios are κα=1/2 and κβ=2, calculate the asymptotic variance and n=400 standard error. List two reasons those calculations could still fail to identify the true population late share.
  8. For the complete (A,D) distribution in Worked example 4, derive the covariance matrix from raw moments and derive the ratio influence without quoting the delta formula. Calculate the correct and independence-assuming variances and explain why a zero observed denominator does not defeat consistency at this fixed law. What changes if the true usage probability is zero?
  9. For iid N(μ,4) observations, derive the limiting law of √n(X̄ₙ²−μ²) at μ=2 and the exact law of nX̄ₙ²/4 at μ=0. Along μₙ=2/√n, give the exact laws of nX̄ₙ²/4 and n(X̄ₙ²−μₙ²)/4. Explain the difference between a zero first-order asymptotic variance and a zero finite-sample estimation error.
  10. In the known-λ Gaussian model, compare λₙ=n−1/4, n−1/2 and n−3/4. Give the exact error variance, determine consistency or failure, and find the normalization producing a standard normal error. Explain why every fixed positive λ can identify θ even though the sequence can be statistically uninformative.
  11. Write the exact binomial-sum coverage event for a Wald interval at p=.6. Reproduce or independently evaluate the three supplied coverages and decide whether their pattern refutes the CLT. State what the “exact” label covers and what the numerical evaluation approximates. Explain why one law and three sample sizes cannot establish uniform coverage over all Bernoulli probabilities.
  12. A report says: “We have a million flagged invoices; the estimated true late fraction is 60%, the optimizer converged, and a 95% interval is narrow, so the payment-reminder program caused delinquency to fall.” Write a research audit distinguishing target, measurement identification, numerical convergence, sampling uncertainty and causal identification. Specify evidence that would change your assessment. An unsupported demand for more rows is not an adequate response.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Order the joint cells (L=1,D=1), (L=1,D=0), (L=0,D=1), (L=0,D=0). The first law gives (4/7,1/7,1/35,9/35); the second gives (18/35,2/35,3/35,12/35). Each vector sums to one and has nonnegative entries. Their flag-one sums both equal 21/35=.6, but actual late shares are 25/35=5/7 and 20/35=4/7. Independent invoice draws therefore give the same observable sample laws. On the error-rate rectangle the derivative signs place the minimum at (.15,.15) and maximum at (.05,.25), giving [9/14,11/14]. Every intermediate value occurs by continuity along a path between the endpoints. This set conditions on the population flag probability; a confidence procedure must account for how p and any validation bounds are estimated. Full credit requires joint-law validity, an explicit identification argument and the set-versus-sampling distinction.
  2. For any ε>0 and n>ε, P(|Xₙ|>ε)=1/n→0. For every realized U>0, eventually n>1/U, so Xₙ=0 forever afterward; almost sure convergence holds as well. E|Xₙ|=1, E[Xₙ²]=n and Var(Xₙ)=n−1. Probability convergence establishes oP(1), which implies OP(1); neither controls these moments. A fixed Z is bounded in probability because its tail probability tends to zero as M→∞, uniformly in n. But P(|Z|>1) is a positive constant, so it cannot converge in probability to zero. The conclusions concern different quantifiers and do not conflict.
  3. Normalize Uₙ=Xₙ/aₙ and Vₙ=Yₙ/bₙ. Choose finite positive M₁,M₂ with each tail eventually below ε/2. Then P(‖UₙVₙ‖>M₁M₂)≤P(‖Uₙ‖>M₁)+P(‖Vₙ‖>M₂)<ε. Independence is not used. For inversion, on |Aₙ−a|<|a|/2, |Aₙ|≥|a|/2 and |1/Aₙ−1/a|≤2|Aₙ−a|/a². The complement probability tends to zero; values assigned on zero events do not alter convergence. Aₙ=1/n is OP(1), but its reciprocal n is not. For fixed-size matrices, convergence in probability to a nonsingular fixed A gives convergence of the inverse on the eventually high-probability nonsingular neighborhood, by the adjugate/determinant argument. Entrywise boundedness alone, or a limiting singular matrix, supplies no such result.
  4. The criterion inequality gives 4‖θ̂−θ₀‖²≤2(.002)+.001=.005, hence ‖θ̂−θ₀‖≤√(.00125)=√2/40≈.035355339 on Eₙ. Thus P(‖θ̂−θ₀‖≤√2/40)≥.97 under the stated event guarantee; nothing makes the displayed radius a data-derived confidence interval if Eₙ's premise has not been justified. The general bound is OP(n−1/4), since 2Δₙ+rₙ=OP(n−1/2). This may be loose. Root-n accuracy requires another argument, such as a local score expansion with nonsingular curvature and appropriate remainder control.
  5. For θ<1, choose n so 1−1/n>θ; then the indicator is zero thereafter. At θ=1 it is zero for every n. The dip is nonempty and every point in it has criterion below zero; its smallest θ minimizes θ² uniquely. Thus θ̂ₙ=1−1/n→1 while Q's unique minimizer is 0. The absolute difference equals 2 inside the dip, so its supremum is 2. The listed finite grid eventually lies outside it. Compactness and continuity of Q hold, and exact sample minimizers exist and are measurable; the missing uniform convergence is the decisive failed condition.
  6. |(W−θ)²−(W−θ′)²|=|θ−θ′||θ+θ′−2W|≤(2B+2|W|)|θ−θ′|. Finite EW² implies E|W|<∞, so L=2B+2|W| is integrable, and q(W,0)=W² is integrable. The finite-net proof therefore applies. Write μ=EW and σ²=Var(W); Q(θ)=σ²+(θ−μ)², uniquely minimized at the Euclidean projection θ₀=max(−B,min(B,μ)). The sample minimizer is the corresponding projection of W̄ and is measurable; consistency also follows directly by continuity. If μ lies outside the interval, the target is the constrained projection, not μ. A structural interpretation would additionally require a model linking W and its mean or projection to the economic parameter; the loss function itself provides none.
  7. Known rates give V=.24/.49=24/49 and SE=√6/70≈.034992711. Differentiating g gives gp=1/d, gα=(p+β−1)/d² and gβ=(p−α)/d², hence (10/7,−20/49,50/49). Equal independent validation sizes yield V=24/49+36/2401+400/2401=1612/2401. With the new ratios, V=24/49+72/2401+200/2401=1448/2401 and SE=√1448/980≈.038829179. The validation groups must represent the relevant conditional recording laws, and their true labels must actually be trustworthy. Time-varying error rates, dependence/overlap, population mismatch, a different operational definition of lateness, or unmodeled selection can invalidate identification or the variance. Two specific justified threats with needed evidence suffice; merely saying “bias” does not.
  8. EA=2, EA²=.2(4)+.2(64)=68/5, giving Var(A)=68/5−4=48/5. ED=ED²=2/5, giving Var(D)=6/25. EAD=EA=2, so Cov(A,D)=2−2(2/5)=6/5. The exact ratio identity μ̂−μ=Pₙ(A−μD)/D̄, consistency of D̄ and the order product yield influence (A−μD)/(.4), with variance 45/2. Dropping covariance gives 60+75/2=195/2, instead of 60−75+75/2=45/2. The arbitrary zero-denominator convention acts on an event with probability (.6)n→0. If p=0, conditional mean E[Y|D=1] is not defined by this observable law and there are no users in the sample; assigning zero to the estimator cannot identify a conditional target on a null event.
  9. At μ=2 and σ²=4, the regular root-n variance is 4μ²σ²=64, so the limit is N(0,64). At μ=0, √nX̄/2 is standard normal exactly, so nX̄²/4 has exactly χ²₁ law for every n. With μₙ=2/√n, √nX̄/2=Z+1, giving nX̄²/4=(Z+1)² and n(X̄²−μₙ²)/4=Z²+2Z. At zero, the unscaled squared-mean error is of order 1/n and remains random; its root-n scaling tends to zero because that scaling is too small to retain the nondegenerate variation. A zero derivative does not imply perfect finite-sample estimation.
  10. The exact error variance is 1/(nλₙ²). For the three sequences it is n−1/2,1 and n1/2, respectively. The first is consistent by Chebyshev or normal tails. The second retains N(0,1) error and fails consistency. In the third the error standard deviation is n1/4, so P(|θ̂−θ|≤ε)=P(|Z|≤ε/n1/4)→0; failure is stronger than merely an inconclusive upper bound. In all three cases √nλₙ(θ̂−θ) is exactly N(0,1), but that normalization shrinks estimation error only when √nλₙ→∞. Different fixed θ values induce different means for every positive λ, proving point identification, yet their separation can shrink too quickly relative to sampling noise along a sequence.
  11. The indicator in the displayed sum is precisely whether p=.6 lies between the estimated lower and upper Wald endpoints, including equality. Summing the Binomial(n,.6) masses over this accepted set gives .936246277,.948117979,.947392305 after rounding. These are model-specific finite-sample coverages; no Monte Carlo uncertainty is involved. The count law and summation formula are exact, while evaluation of the normal quantile and decimal display is numerical. Their mild nonmonotonicity does not contradict convergence as n→∞. Near p=0 or 1 the plug-in variance degenerates and the quality can differ sharply; a universal or uniform claim requires a separate analysis over that range, not extrapolation from these three cases.
  12. Illustrative audit. Define actual lateness using a due-date rule, population and period; distinguish it from D. Obtain externally validated error rates or defensible bounds and check their transport to the million invoices. A converged optimizer addresses a criterion and tolerance, not whether the target is identified or whether the criterion corresponds to lateness. Determine the independent sampling units and dependence across customers, time or billing systems; a million rows may represent far fewer independent pieces of information. A confidence interval needs a justified estimator expansion and variance, and a narrow interval around a misidentified target is still misleading. A causal reminder effect requires an explicit treatment contrast and assignment/counterfactual argument: for example a documented randomized rollout with an appropriate estimand, or a separately defended observational design addressing selection and common trends. Audit nonresponse, measurement changes, timing and specification selection. Useful new evidence includes validation records, sampling/assignment logs, an unchanged outcome definition and a pre-specified comparison. Full credit requires all five distinctions, concrete evidence requests, and conditional conclusions; no particular policy conclusion is required.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In five minutes, explain why an infinitely precise flag frequency can leave actual late payment unidentified, then derive the corrected estimator's standard error under known recording rates. Explain where the derivative and sampling covariance enter, and why a boundary projection changes the limiting law. A satisfactory explanation gives two observationally equivalent mechanisms, the identifying inversion, the centered CLT and a clear distinction between the normal and positive-part limits.

Delayed check, after 7–14 days. Without the chapter, take p=.55, α=.05, β=.15 and n=625. Derive the known-rate target and asymptotic standard error; state the approximate-minimizer consistency conditions; and explain why an estimator that is consistent at every fixed positive λ can fail along λₙ=n−1/2. The delay is an authored practice suggestion, not a calibrated retention guarantee.

Retention solution and repair map

The target is (.55−.05)/(.8)=5/8. Bernoulli variance is 99/400, so corrected root-n variance is 99/256 and SE=√99/400≈.024874686. Compact Θ, continuous Q with a unique minimizer, measurable uniform criterion error oP(1), and a measurable approximate minimizer with nonnegative objective error oP(1) give consistency by the positive-gap inequality. Fixed positive λ supplies a shrinking variance 1/(nλ²); λₙ=n−1/2 leaves it equal to one. If the target was confused with the flag, revisit Section 1; for a missing centering or unsupported reciprocal, Section 2; for an optimizer-based consistency claim, Section 3; for a wrong scale or omitted covariance, Sections 4–5; for a universal normal approximation, Section 6. Reconstruct the failed argument with a new number or model, rather than memorizing this answer.

Sources, proof boundaries and next study

The three cited primary MIT course sources supply the scoped limit, extremum and delta framework. Aldous's Berkeley lecture notes, recorded by Chewi, supply the explicitly invoked joint-convergence characterization. Our calculations, financial cases, counterexamples, proofs and problems are original. The compact approximate-minimizer and Lipschitz finite-net arguments are proved here; iid scalar mean laws and the scalar CLT were proved in the prerequisite chapter. The general finite-dimensional Cramér–Wold characterization is explicitly invoked. We have not proved a general dependent-data CLT, empirical-process equicontinuity theorem, high-dimensional Gaussian approximation, or uniform inference over weakly identified models.

Next, linear models connect these tools to projection, exact conditional covariance, feasible weighting and inference under heteroskedasticity, clusters and serial dependence. Each dependence model needs its own effective sampling units and valid limit argument. Later chapters examine weak instruments, nonlinear estimation and causal research designs; the target, identification and uncertainty distinctions established here continue to govern each application.

Sources and further study

  • Anna Mikusheva, MIT 14.381 — Lecture 2: Limit Theorems (Fall 2018) — Finite-variance LLN, scalar/vector CLT statements, probability versus distribution convergence, stochastic orders, Slutsky and first-order delta reasoning. Original chapter proofs/examples must state their own assumptions.
  • Victor Chernozhukov, MIT 14.385 — Lecture 2: Consistency for Extremum Estimators (Fall 2007) — Separation plus uniform criterion convergence as sufficient conditions for consistency. Chapter will independently prove a finite-dimensional compact approximate-minimizer result and a bounded/Lipschitz finite-net ULLN.
  • Peter Kempthorne, MIT 18.655 — Lecture 16: Asymptotics, Consistency and Delta Method (Spring 2016) — Consistent plug-in functionals, first-order differentiability remainder and studentized mean. Original exact examples will distinguish weak distributional limits from convergence of moments.
  • David Aldous, Probability Theory (Berkeley C205B/C218B, Spring 2017), notes by Sinho Chewi — Lecture 8, Cramér–Wold device — Direct support for the explicitly invoked finite-dimensional Cramér–Wold characterization; scalar projections identify a joint limit when a matching vector law exists. The chapter derives its scalar-contrast limits and constructs the Gaussian candidate from a covariance square root.
